p01.text: On March 26 the Israeli military said Revolutionary Guards navy commander Alireza Tangsiri had been killed in an airstrike in Bandar Abbas, and the Revolutionary Guards confirmed it. He had led the navy since 2018 and directed the blockade of Hormuz. The same day two teenagers were killed in strikes on homes in Shiraz, and in Abu Dhabi two civilians were killed by debris from an intercepted Iranian missile. The gatekeeper of the strait had been erased.

p02.text: Bellingcat said that before dawn on March 26 U.S. forces appeared to have scattered antitank mines over the village of Kafari near Shiraz. Experts identified them as mines from the GATOR system. It was the first combat use of scatterable antitank mines by the United States since the 1991 Gulf War. A missile base lay about two kilometers away. A thirty-one-year-old father was killed after picking up a mine that had fallen next to his car.

p03.text: The same day President Trump claimed Iran’s leaders were “begging” for a peace deal. Iran denied negotiating. The Revolutionary Guards announced a program called “For Iran,” allowing recruitment for security duties from the age of twelve. On March 11 an eleven-year-old boy had been killed at a Tehran checkpoint. Lebanon’s Health Ministry said the death toll since Israel’s invasion had risen to 1,116, and two Golani Brigade soldiers were killed.

p04.text: On March 27 Iranian missiles and drones struck Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, south of Riyadh, home to U.S. tankers and early warning aircraft. Fifteen U.S. troops were wounded, five of them critically. Several aerial refueling tankers and one E-3 airborne early warning and control aircraft were damaged. In an earlier attack that same week, fourteen U.S. troops were also reported wounded. The blood of this war was running on other people’s land.

p05.text: The same day drones and missiles hit Kuwait’s Shuwaikh and Mubarak Al-Kabeer ports. The UAE intercepted six ballistic missiles and nine drones. Iranian cluster munitions fell on six sites in central Israel, and one person was killed in Ramat Gan. There are three parties to this war, but missiles and drones have fallen on more than ten countries. On March 11 the Security Council condemned Iran’s attacks on its Gulf neighbors and Jordan.

p06.text: One line on the status board changed. Lieutenant Kim Junho had been watching that line for twenty-seven days. The Revolutionary Guards navy commander, Tangsiri. The man who sorted the ships that could pass from the ships that would be hit. This morning the box next to his name said KIA presumed. He thought of the Vincennes on this sea in 1988. The one who is frightened shoots first. Henderson gave a short whistle. “The man holding the key ring is gone. Isn’t that good news for your ships?”

p07.text: “I don’t know, sir. He was the man who picked which ships got through. When somebody called, he was the one who picked up. Now who picks up that phone?” One captain had five days of water left. The part he needed was in Dubai, a hundred and twenty nautical miles away. It is easy to believe that if you kill the gatekeeper the gate will open. But the only one who knew where the key was hanging was the gatekeeper.

p08.text: Four thirty in the morning, noon in Tehran. Leila Shirazi finished her analysis of the five conditions and called her aunt. The line went through on the third try. What piece of this war her cables had made, she could not tell her aunt. “Auntie. I’m sorry.” “For what?” “Just because.” A pot lid rattled. “Just because isn’t just because, Leila.” Leila hung up first. If she heard any more she would come apart.

p09.text: Back at her desk there was a new post up. The president said Iran’s leaders were begging for a deal. The side that is told it is begging fires something to show it is not. She wrote two readings into the cable. Those who want to talk and those who want to fire are split. Warning: insulting public language weakens the side that wants to talk. Someone up the chain might strike that line. She did not. The sentences she did not delete were adding up.

p10.text: They came down in the night. Hasan was sixty-three and had grown pomegranates and wheat in this village all his life. One by the road. One by the ditch. One under the fig tree. Like flat cans, grass-colored, with a fin on one side. In the Iran-Iraq War he had learned one thing. Anything that falls from the sky and does not go off has not finished its work. He shouted. Don’t come out. Don’t touch anything.

p11.text: There was a dull sound at the edge of the village. He did not run. Thirty meters took five minutes. The young father’s car, a child’s school bag on the back seat. Somebody on a map had drawn a line. That a pomegranate orchard and a child’s way to school lay on that line was not on the map. A bomb kills people the day it falls. A mine waits where it is after the war is over. Until the pomegranates ripen. Until the child goes back to school.

p12.text: Colonel Darius Sepahvand had not slept at all. In the morning there was a one-line text from a number he did not know. Baba, I’m okay. Where she was, who she was with, whether she had water. Nothing. He read the line a hundred times. After a hundred times it was still one line. At noon an order came down. Recruitment from the age of twelve. He put it on the desk. It was not his hand that was shaking. It was the paper.

p13.text: When Narges was twelve, she would try on her father’s uniform cap before she got out of the car. The cap was big. It came down over her eyes. She laughed. What he had spent thirty-one years trying to protect was not a country that put that cap on a child and stood her at a checkpoint. On March 11 an eleven-year-old boy had died at a Tehran checkpoint, and Amnesty International called the mobilization of children a war crime.

p14.text: In 1987 his older brother died on the southern front, a seventeen-year-old volunteer. He went with a plastic key around his neck. The key to paradise, they said. Thirteen-year-old Darius watched their mother get the key back and put it in a drawer. Eight years later he put on the uniform his brother should have worn, swearing no seventeen-year-old would ever die like that again. His brother was not the only boy with a key like that.

p15.text: For thirty-one years he had never taken out that vow. Today he did. The vow had died long ago. Darius made his decision. He had a head that knew this command post’s network, and the memory of a cable: the coordinates of the Fordow air-defense zone, and three lines on what was spinning under that mountain. The country he had meant to protect was outside it. Getting out takes longer than getting in. First you have to find the door.

p16.text: Nariman brought the atlas she had saved from the house that fell, its cover swollen with water. “Here. Abu Dhabi. They said two people died here today. Who shot that missile?” Professor Azad Moradi stopped for a moment. “Iran shot it.” “We did? Why did we?” To a seven-year-old the country was we. For seventy-two years he had used that word carefully. He knew too well who this country’s “we” put in and who it left out.

p17.text: “Because there are American soldiers there.” “But the people who died weren’t American soldiers.” “In a war the reasons are complicated, Nariman.” “If it’s complicated, then just don’t do it.” Azad could not answer. Evening light came in through the ventilation window. Spring was coming, even in a war. That was the logic of nature, simpler than the logic of people, and older. A seven-year-old’s logic beat the grown-ups’ war.

p18.text: Captain Marcus Webb read the casualty report twice. Prince Sultan. Fifteen. Five critical. The tankers that fueled his aircraft flew from there. He did not know their faces. He knew their voices on the radio. A boom operator with a Texas accent always said the same thing when the refueling was done. Fly safe, Navy. Whether that man was among the fifteen, he had no way to know. His ship was heading to Croatia for repairs.

p19.text: Two countries started this war, and the blood was running in ten. A base in Saudi Arabia, a worker in Abu Dhabi, the ports of Kuwait. An alliance came down to this: lending your land to someone else’s war, and paying the rent in your own people’s blood. He called the Bahrain number. “This is Webb. Last time I said ‘not yet.’ I’m moving that up. Leave out the name.” The treaties write the obligations, and the blood soaks into a desert runway.

p20.text: Three in the morning. Only Captain Farhan Moradi was on duty. “I can’t sleep. Let’s have some tea.” The console still held one line from joint anti-smuggling work before the war, running through a relay station in Quetta to Islamabad. For twenty-eight days no one had used it. No one had cut it, either. “Did you see the order that came down today? Twelve.” Farhan’s laugh stopped. He answered by not answering.

p21.text: “My uncle used to say what’s frightening about soldiers is that they hand their thinking over to someone else. These days I’m not so sure.” Betrayal and loyalty begin with the same sentence: I am trying to protect this country. It is the next sentence where they part. In Seoul, Kang Yujin told her lab director Park Sejun about the model reacting to a variable she had not put in. “Who have you told?” His nod went on a little long.
